subject: physics
question_text: Define the coefficient of thermal conductivity and derive an expression for the rate of heat conduction through a slab. A copper bar 10 cm long, of cross-sectional area 1 mm², has its ends kept at 104 °C and 24 °C. Find the rate at which heat is conducted along the bar. (K for copper = 401 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.)

mark_split.label: Heat conducted and the rate of flow

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 11 Long Answer Question, printed p.119. Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The eight 1-mark step split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: P = KA(T₁ − T₂)/L with K = 401 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, A = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m², T₁ − T₂ = 80 (the same number in °C and K), and L = 0.10 m gives P = 0.32 W.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Definition of conduction
lines: Thermal conduction is the transfer
of heat through a body, from its
hotter part to its colder part,
without the material itself moving.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say heat moves from the hotter part to the colder part without the material moving.
steps.why: This is the defining feature of conduction: the heat itself travels through the fixed material, unlike convection, where the material moves, or radiation, which needs no material at all.
common_mistakes: Describing the heat as carried by the moving material, which is convection rather than conduction.
Leaving out that the body itself does not move.

recall.must_convey: That conduction is heat transfer through a body from its hotter part to its colder part, without the material itself moving.
accept: heat moves from the hot part to the cold part
conduction transfers heat without the material moving
heat passes through a fixed body
reject: heat is carried by moving material

steps.memory_tip: Conduction: the heat travels, the material stays still.

steps.label: Coefficient of thermal conductivity
lines: The coefficient of thermal
conductivity K is the rate of flow
of heat per unit area per unit
temperature gradient across the slab.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. State that K is the rate of heat flow per unit area per unit temperature gradient.
steps.why: Defining K here, before the slab equation is derived, means the derivation can name K as an already-known constant of proportionality, rather than using an undefined symbol.
common_mistakes: Defining K only as how well a material conducts heat, without the per unit area, per unit gradient part.
Confusing K with specific heat, which is a different constant entirely.

recall.must_convey: That K, the coefficient of thermal conductivity, is the rate of flow of heat per unit area per unit temperature gradient.
accept: K is heat flow per unit area per unit gradient
coefficient of thermal conductivity
rate of heat flow per area per gradient

steps.memory_tip: K: heat flow, per area, per degree of gradient.

steps.label: SI unit of K
lines: The SI unit of K is W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.
A large value of K means the
material is a good conductor of heat.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Give the SI unit W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, and note that a large K means a good conductor.
steps.why: The unit W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ follows from how K was just defined — a rate of heat flow, per unit area, per unit temperature gradient — and stating what a large K means gives the definition physical content.
common_mistakes: Giving the unit without its exponents, writing W m K instead of W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Reversing the meaning of K and calling a small K a good conductor.

recall.must_convey: That the SI unit of K is W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, and a large K means a good conductor of heat.
accept: watt per metre per kelvin
W m to the minus one K to the minus one
a large K is a good conductor

steps.memory_tip: W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ — power, per metre, per kelvin.

steps.label: Deriving the heat conduction formula
lines: For a slab of area A and thickness
L, with its faces kept at T₁ and T₂,
the heat conducted Q in time t obeys:

lines.text: Q ∝ A, Q ∝ (T₁ − T₂), Q ∝ t, Q ∝ 1 / L

lines: Combining these four, with K as
the constant of proportionality,
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Combine Q ∝ A, Q ∝ (T₁ − T₂), Q ∝ t and Q ∝ 1/L into Q = KA(T₁ − T₂)t / L.
steps.why: The question asks the student to DERIVE the expression, not assume it: Q depends directly on the area, the temperature difference and the time, and inversely on the thickness, so combining these four proportions with K, already defined, as the constant of proportionality is what makes this step a derivation.
common_mistakes: Writing the final formula directly, without showing the four proportions that combine to give it.
Getting one proportion inverted, such as writing Q ∝ L instead of Q ∝ 1/L.

recall.must_convey: That Q ∝ A, Q ∝ (T₁ − T₂), Q ∝ t and Q ∝ 1/L, and combining these four proportions with K as the constant of proportionality gives Q = KA(T₁ − T₂)t / L.
accept: Q is proportional to area, to the temperature difference and to time, and inversely proportional to thickness
combining the four proportions with K gives Q equals K A delta T t over L
Q proportional to A, delta T, t, and one over L

steps.memory_tip: Q ∝ A, ΔT and t; Q ∝ 1/L — combine with K.

steps.label: Heat conducted and the rate of flow
lines: The heat conducted is therefore
and the rate of conduction is Q
divided by the time t:
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. State Q = KA(T₁ − T₂)t / L, then divide by t to reach the rate P = KA(T₁ − T₂) / L.
steps.why: The question asks for a RATE of heat conduction, so this step takes the derived heat Q and divides it by the time t to reach the power P — the quantity the numerical part of the question actually calculates.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as Q instead of dividing by t to reach the rate P.
Writing P = KA(T₁ − T₂) × L instead of KA(T₁ − T₂) / L.

recall.must_convey: That Q = KA(T₁ − T₂)t / L, and dividing by t gives the rate P = Q/t = KA(T₁ − T₂) / L.
accept: Q equals K A delta T t over L
P equals Q over t
dividing by time gives the rate K A delta T over L
reject: Q proportional to A, delta T, t, and one over L
heard_as: Q equals K A delta T t over L

steps.memory_tip: P is Q per second: divide the derived formula by t.

steps.label: Values for the copper bar
lines: For the copper bar, K = 401 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹,
T₁ = 104 °C and T₂ = 24 °C, so
A difference of 80 is the same
number in °C and in K, because the
two scales have degrees of the same size.
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Write the given values, and note ΔT = 80 is the same number in °C and in K.
steps.why: The formula uses a temperature DIFFERENCE. A difference of one degree Celsius is the same size as a difference of one kelvin, so ΔT = 80 can be used directly, without converting either end temperature to kelvin first.
common_mistakes: Believing the temperature difference itself changes value when converted to kelvin — it does not; converting both end temperatures first is valid, just unnecessary extra work.
Subtracting the temperatures the wrong way round, getting ΔT = −80.

recall.must_convey: That K = 401 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, L = 0.10 m, A = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m², and ΔT = T₁ − T₂ = 80, the same number in °C and in K.
accept: K is 401, L is 0.10 metres, A is one times ten to minus six
delta T is 80
80 degrees Celsius is the same as 80 kelvin for a difference
the difference does not change when converted to kelvin
reject: P equals K A delta T over L
heard_as: one times ten to the minus six

steps.memory_tip: A difference of degrees is the same number in °C or K — only a single temperature needs +273.

steps.label: Substitute the values
lines: Substitute into P = KA(T₁ − T₂)/L:
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Substitute K = 401, A = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶, ΔT = 80, L = 0.10 into the rate formula.
steps.why: This step turns the general formula into a single arithmetic expression, ready to be worked out to a number in the next step.
common_mistakes: Substituting the length in centimetres, 10, instead of converting it to 0.10 m first.
Substituting the area in mm², 1.0, instead of converting it to 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² first.

recall.must_convey: That substituting K = 401, A = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m², ΔT = 80, L = 0.10 m into P = KA(T₁ − T₂)/L gives P = 401 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 80 / 0.10.
accept: substitute 401, one times ten to minus six, 80 and 0.10
put the numbers into the rate formula
401 times area times delta T over L
heard_as: 401 times 1 times ten to minus six

steps.memory_tip: Keep every length in metres and every area in m² before you substitute.

steps.label: The rate of heat conducted
lines: Dividing by 0.10,
steps.margin_note: Eighth mark. Show 401 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 80 = 3.208 × 10⁻², then divide by 0.10 to state P = 0.32 W.
steps.why: The complete answer states the rate as a number with its unit, watts, which is what the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as a decimal without its unit, watts.

recall.must_convey: That evaluating the substituted expression gives P = 0.32 W.
accept: P equals 0.32 watts
the rate of heat conducted is 0.32 watts
zero point three two watts

steps.memory_tip: 0.32 W — a small rate, because the bar's cross section is only 1 mm².

insider_note: The complete answer keeps the temperature difference as 80 throughout, the same number in °C and in K. Converting both end temperatures to kelvin first gives the same 80 K difference and is equally valid — it is simply unnecessary extra work when only the difference is needed.
